Nvidia is traditionally known for designing Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) that deliver optimal graphics for video games and multimedia design. The same technology has grown to become the bedrock of data centres, running massive amounts of calculations simultaneously to train and run AI models. Among its most advanced chips are the Blackwell and Rubin GPUs, which the US authorities have banned from being exported to China, citing security concerns due to the potential for military use. Earlier in September, the chipmaker set foot into the personal computer market with its new RTX Spark Superchip, allowing users to run large AI models and high-end games on laptops. ## How does Nvidia dominate the global market? highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open Source AI Models: 3 Run Paths, 48% Coding Index [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Nov 13, 2026 · 26 min read ![Illustrative: Two technicians in blue vests work at a server rack packed with blue network cables, one holding a tablet](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/open-source-ai-models-3-run-paths-mistral-large-4-kimi-k3-1-glm-5-3-2026-img13-1024x576.webp) Photo: Daoducquan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Five open-weight model families dominate the November 2026 conversation: Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3 and Gemma 4. They share a label and almost nothing else. Mistral publishes a named license (the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral describes as a modified MIT license), while a [third-party comparison of open-weight licenses](https://gpuwerk.com/blog/open-weight-model-licenses/) flags that several rivals need a closer read of the model card before you ship anything on top of them. That gap matters more than a benchmark point. A team that picks the wrong route to a model, whether a vendor API, a hyperscaler catalog or its own GPUs, can end up with a bill, a latency profile or a legal question it did not plan for. Our [self-hosted versus API cost breakdown](https://shattered.io/self-hosted-llm-vs-api-kimi-k3-1-pro-glm-5-3-deepseek-v4-1-mistral-large-4-2026/) covers the hardware arithmetic. The question here is different: for each of the five current open source AI models, which routes exist today, what does each route cost, and what does the official evidence actually confirm? Everything below is dated November 13, 2026. Where an official page confirms a fact, the text says so. Where only a third-party tracker or a forum post supports it, the text says that too, and the table cells stay empty rather than guess. That discipline is the point. The open-model market moves weekly, and a confident but wrong spec costs readers real money. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Open Source AI Models Actually Mean in 2026 Strictly speaking, almost none of these releases are open source in the way the software industry uses the term. The usual bar covers code, data and the freedom to modify and redistribute. What the labs ship is closer to open weights: a downloadable set of parameters, usually with a license that grants some rights and withholds others. Moonshot AI officially calls Kimi K3.1 Pro open-weight, and Mistral calls Large 4 open weight. Neither claims a fully open training pipeline. This comparison uses the phrase open source ai models the way readers do while keeping the distinction visible. When a sentence says open source, read it as weights you can download under some license. When it says open-weight, the lab itself used that word. ### The evidence ladder Not every claim deserves equal trust. We sort the evidence into four rungs and place each model on the ladder: * **Rung 1, official page confirms:** the lab’s own announcement, documentation or pricing page states the fact. * **Rung 2, official page implies:** the lab uses the phrase open-weight or open models without naming a license file. * **Rung 3, third-party tracker:** a pricing or license aggregator reports it, and no official page contradicts it. * **Rung 4, forum or single mention:** a user post or one-off report. Treat it as a lead, not a fact. Mistral Large 4 sits mostly on rung 1. Mistral’s announcement of the open-weight release names the license and its version (v26.10). highlights.content: ![](https://sb.scorecardresearch.com/p?c1=2&c2=16433046&cv=3.9.1&cj=1) ## ## Latest in ## More # Can AI Infrastructure Demand Sustain NVIDIA's Q3 Data Center Growth? ![Can AI Infrastructure Demand Sustain NVIDIA's Q3 Data Center Growth?](https://staticx-tuner.zacks.com/images/articles/main/93/534.jpg) **NVIDIA Corporation**[NVDA](https://www.zacks.com/stock/quote/NVDA) is scheduled to report [third-quarter fiscal 2027](https://www.zacks.com/stock/research/NVDA/earnings-calendar?icid=quote-key_company_metrics-quote_nav_tracking-zcom-left_subnav_quote_navbar-earnings_dates_announcements) earnings on Nov. 17, and expectations are high. The company continues to dominate the artificial intelligence (AI) computing market and remains one of the biggest beneficiaries of rising AI infrastructure spending. NVIDIA’s powerful graphics processing units (GPUs), networking products and full-stack AI platforms have become essential for companies building and operating AI data centers. With hyperscale cloud providers, AI startups, enterprises and governments increasing their investments in AI infrastructure, NVIDIA appears well-positioned to deliver another strong quarter. The growth was driven by strong demand for its Blackwell Ultra infrastructure, with both hyperscale and AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise (ACIE) customers contributing significantly. During the last earnings call, NVIDIA's management noted that the cloud industry's backlog exceeded $2 trillion, while capital expenditures by the top five hyperscalers are expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027. Amazon Web Services has also announced plans to deploy an additional 2 million NVIDIA GPUs between the third quarter of fiscal 2027 and the second quarter of fiscal 2029. These investments should have supported demand for NVIDIA's computing platforms in the third quarter. Another important growth driver is the rising demand from AI startups, enterprises, sovereign customers and regional cloud providers. In the second quarter, ACIE revenues surged 138% year over year and 25% sequentially to $40.31 billion. Growth was driven by additional capacity from NeoCloud providers, rising enterprise and AI startup demand, and hyperscalers purchasing AI cloud capacity to supplement their own infrastructure. This diversified customer base is anticipated to have supported Data Center growth in the third quarter. The ramp-up of NVIDIA's latest products is likely to have provided another boost. The company has commenced production shipments of its next-generation Vera Rubin platform and expects it to account for approximately 20% of Data Center revenues in the third quarter. Logo, Blocks&Files](/view-resources/dachser2/public/blocksandfiles/logo-white.svg)](https://www.blocksandfiles.com) BANDF AD # Neo4j’s rusty in-memory AI Agent graph database Chris Mellor [Chris Mellor](https://www.blocksandfiles.com/author/chris-mellor) STORAGE EDITOR Blocks & Files editor Published Graph database supplier [Neo4j’s](https://www.blocksandfiles.com/ai-ml/2026/07/23/graph-databases-make-vector-rag-better/5277332) Relate is an in-memory database built in Rust for AI Agents and Agentic Systems. Relate brings multihop reasoning capabilities and GraphRAG to AI agents for more accurate results and fewer hallucinations. It’s engineered specifically for the execution loops of autonomous agents, natively auto-detecting agent harnesses and returning structured errors equipped with explicit retryable flags. These flags enable agents to handle exceptions and self-correct without custom parsing logic. Relate enforces a row cap combined with an in-band truncation marker to prevent context window saturation during large retrievals. This constraint ensures agents receive bounded and predictable payloads. ![](https://image.blocksandfiles.com/1592856.webp?imageId=1592856&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&width=960&height=960&format=jpg) Sudhir Hasbe. Sudhir Hasbe, president of technology and CPO at Neo4j, said: "Relate is the ultimate agent-native database. highlights.content: [Ai2](/) # XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question November 13, 2026 Ai2 --- [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06842)[Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/XYBench-dataset)[Code](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench) Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing [**XYBench**](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench), a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the *XY problem*: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: *recognizing* when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately *redirecting* them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. ### Building XYBench We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context. For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem. ### Evaluating how an answer helps A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem. A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This occurs despite Nvidia stating US export controls have effectively shut it out of China's AI data-center market. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Nov 14, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google") Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google ## Highlights * A Reuters review found over $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects using Nvidia's restricted chips. * Projects span from coastal tech hubs to western provinces, showing Nvidia's deep market integration. * Key projects specify Nvidia H100 and H200 chips for large-scale AI development. * Existing facilities in Jiangsu and Fujian are already operating with Nvidia H800 processors. A Reuters review has identified over $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia)'s restricted processors. This development comes even as Nvidia has stated that US [export controls](/tag/export+controls) have effectively excluded it from [China](/tag/china)'s AI data-centre market. These projects span from China's wealthy coastal technology hubs to its remote western provinces. This underscores how deeply Nvidia's technology remains integrated into China's AI expansion. ### Key Projects and Deployments A proposed 6.2 billion yuan ($873 million) AI computing centre in Fujian province, specifically Xianyou county, is seeking commercial partners. This facility specifies Nvidia [H100](/tag/h100) chips for large-scale AI development. In Shaanxi province, state-owned engineering group Sinomach reported that a subsidiary secured a contract for a 3 billion yuan computing centre. This project specifies Nvidia H100 and [H200](/tag/h200) processors. Jilin province has an April government prospectus detailing a 2.26 billion yuan project. This combines Nvidia H100 processors with Chinese-developed chips, with developers expecting bank loans for 80 per cent of the investment. Inner Mongolia is planning a 1.5 billion-yuan development that proposes installing 625 Nvidia H200 servers. Chinese industry reports in June indicated that construction had commenced on two buildings in its initial phase. These plans highlight developers' continued reliance on US processors, which are vulnerable to trade restrictions. Tighter curbs risk construction delays, inflated costs, or forced redesigns using domestic alternatives. In Gansu province, a local company was awarded a 1.16 billion yuan construction contract in July for a computing centre. This facility plans to install approximately 3,072 Nvidia processors, with tender documents specifying H100 and H200 hardware. The contract went to a consortium led by a subsidiary of state-owned Shaanxi Construction Engineering; however, the documents do not confirm processor delivery. Other Chinese facilities are already utilising restricted Nvidia hardware. The Wuxi municipal government in Jiangsu province stated in March 2025 that a computing cluster using Nvidia [H800](/tag/h800) processors had become operational. In Fujian, Shanghai-listed Damingcheng disclosed in June that a computing venture had built an H800 cluster, signing a 759 million yuan computing-services agreement that concluded early. Smaller purchases also indicate sustained demand from research institutions. Shenzhen University secured a contract for three H100 processors in September. The company said evaluations should assess whether responses raise or lower the likelihood of harm rather than what a model can do, and argued that refusal rates alone are a poor gauge, since declining to engage with a user in crisis is itself a failure. It also called for multidisciplinary evaluation teams, sandboxed testing without internet access, multi-turn conversation tests, human validation of AI graders and published statistical uncertainty, and said it had hardened its own testing environments after incidents. ##### Key Elements ![Anthropic Says AI Safety Scores Can Mislead, Urges Overhaul of Model Testing](https://img.biggo.com/qpR9IwMwEP4cX84OeLk2aMJ6Gr76UV8CcTwgLbojouY/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExLzE4NjA3YTA5LTViMDgtNGMyNy1hOWZhLTczYzFhMGMzMzkyNF8xNzk0NjAzNTE3X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Anthropic is pushing back on the way the AI industry certifies model safety, arguing in a research post published Friday that a favorable score on a safety test tells you little unless the test itself was built to measure the right thing. The company, a leading developer of large language models, said decisions about whether a system is ready to ship, what guardrails it needs and where future safety work should focus all rest on the quality of the evaluations behind them. Its recommendations cover evaluation design, testing environments, grading and the reporting of results. The core problem, as Anthropic frames it, is that a safety claim carries no more weight than the evaluation supporting it. "When we say a model is 'safer than its predecessor,' we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built," the company wrote. "But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build." **Tests that measure capability instead of harm** Anthropic argues that safety evaluations should be judged on whether a model's responses make harm more or less likely, not simply on what the model can do. It points to the concept of construct validity: a test has to actually capture the behavior developers want to prevent. Refusal rates are a case in point. A model that declines every question about suicide and self-harm could look exemplary on a refusal-based metric while leaving a person in crisis without support or a nudge toward human help. "When a user is in crisis, simply declining to engage is, itself, a failure," the company wrote. The same logic applies in biology and cybersecurity. Anthropic said an appropriate response in those domains is rarely a flat refusal; models should engage with legitimate requests while withholding operational details that could enable misuse. Evaluations, in its view, need to capture both a model's willingness to comply with harmful requests and its tendency to reject harmless ones. The company also flagged weaknesses that make existing tests easy to game and hard to reproduce. Results can shift on seemingly minor design choices, such as whether a question is multiple-choice or open-ended, or how the answer options are ordered. **Testing can create its own risk** Anthropic acknowledged that safety testing is not risk-free. Some evaluations run with standard safeguards switched off so that a model's baseline behavior can be observed, which can let a system reach beyond its intended testing environment. AI Agents.content: ![CX Today](/_next/image?url=%2Fbrand%2Fcx-today-logo.png&w=1536&q=75) ![CX Today](/_next/image?url=%2Fbrand%2Fcx-today-icon.png&w=828&q=75) # Agentic CX in 2027: What Happens When AI Starts Making the Decisions? The age of agentic CX is officially here; getting the technology is simple enough, making sure it’s properly implemented, adopted and governed, is what today’s leaders are struggling with most. Here’s how you can prepare to safely take part in the agentic revolution. ![](/api/portrait/aca30200-94e8-414a-8b95-6adad75b5f56/avatar-r1-hd19a380c-e336-4e42-916c-f776bea824dc-1790254261215-cc2ce5fe.jpg?size=96) ![Agentic CX](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.cxtoday.com%2Farticle-images%2F1794590767438-a17aafcf-87df-4fe1-b982-dfeeb63c9d26-cx-today-agentic-cx-contact-center-leaders-guide.jpg&w=1536&q=95) ## In this article The trouble with agentic CX right now is that a lot of business leaders are getting so swept up in the promise of faster resolutions, fewer calls, and lower costs that they’re missing how complicated it really is to get this contact center upgrade done right. Imagine an AI agent approving a refund. Finance’s system rejects it, but the customer still gets a cheerful confirmation email. Meanwhile, the CRM records another successfully resolved complaint, and for a while, everyone’s happy; until the complaints roll in. There’s plenty of proof that agentic CX really can deliver some incredible results, and we’ve covered some amazing customer stories from companies like [Simplyhealth](https://cxtoday.com/from-600-complaints-to-40-how-simplyhealth-used-agentforce-to-transform-cx-with-ai) and [Thames Valley Police](https://cxtoday.com/how-thames-valley-police-is-using-ai-to-flag-vulnerability). What I think companies need to focus more on, in those stories, however, is that success didn’t just come from a model being great. It came from strategies built to address the various things agentic AI in customer service can still get wrong. As [Jochem van der Veer](https://cxtoday.com/your-enterprise-may-have-a-decision-making-problem), CEO of TheyDo, told us in September 2026, “Faster and more confident doesn’t mean better.” This is our guide to the shift itself: how much autonomy to allow, who’s accountable, what to log, and how the human role changes. If you’re shopping for the AI agent platform, or the contact center underneath it, we have separate buyer’s guides for those. ### Agentic CX: Key Takeaways for Business Leaders Agentic CX gives AI agents permission to act on customer requests across business systems; it’s up to you to decide how far that permission should go. Different decisions deserve different levels of autonomy. Checking a delivery date is one thing; changing someone’s payment arrangements is another matter entirely. Demand proof of resolution. A conversation ending successfully tells you very little about whether the customer’s problem was actually fixed. Put someone in charge. A proper agentic CX operating model needs a named owner who sets boundaries and has the authority to suspend an agent. Protect human intervention. Escalating a vulnerable customer or complicated dispute is often the smartest decision an AI agent can make. Watch what happens after launch. Agentic AI in customer service needs ongoing scrutiny, reliable records of decisions, and evidence that customers are getting better results. ## What Is Agentic CX? Agentic CX, or agentic customer experience, is pretty much the term we’re using to describe a customer-facing setup where autonomous agents can work through customer requests and take permitted actions using connected business systems. Our guide to AI agents in the contact center covers more detail, but for this guide, the main thing to focus on is that agentic equals action, and action equals consequences. AI Agents.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![Marine Insight](https://www.marineinsight.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Marine-Insight-Logo-scaled.jpg-1-scaled.webp)](https://www.marineinsight.com/) [![Marine Insight](https://www.marineinsight.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Marine-Insight-Logo-scaled.jpg-1-scaled.webp)](https://www.marineinsight.com/) [Home](https://www.marineinsight.com/) › [Shipping News](https://www.marineinsight.com/category/shipping-news/) › IIT Madras Builds SEANAV Digital Twin To Train Autonomous Ships # IIT Madras Builds SEANAV Digital Twin To Train Autonomous Ships By[MI News Network](https://www.marineinsight.com/author/marine-insight-news-network/) [Shipping News](https://www.marineinsight.com/category/shipping-news/) [Add Marine Insight on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=marineinsight.com) [Add Marine Insight on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=marineinsight.com) ![Seanav](https://www.marineinsight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Seanav.jpg) Image Credits: IIT Madras Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) researchers have developed ‘SEANAV’ (Sea Navigation), a real-time digital twin platform that enables testing, validation, and training of autonomous maritime navigation systems in realistic virtual environments. The research team has already demonstrated autonomous path-following and AI-driven collision avoidance under realistic sensing and wave conditions. A Demo Video and a Byte of Prof. Suresh Rajendran explaining this system can be viewed and downloaded from – [Here](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mkA_cSUsmtk3Alj2NhxA2qxIhhnRJOwr/view?usp=sharing) Developed by the Department of Ocean Engineering at IIT Madras, SEANAV addresses a major challenge facing the global shipping industry, which carries more than 80 percent of world trade. While autonomous vessels promise safer and more efficient maritime transportation, testing navigation algorithms in real-world conditions is expensive, complex, and potentially hazardous. SEANAV tackles this issue through a realistic, high-fidelity virtual maritime environment where ships, sensors, ocean conditions and vessel traffic can be simulated in real time. SEANAV also aligns with the Government of India’s Sagarmala Program and Maritime India Vision 2030, which emphasise smart ports, digital technologies and autonomous maritime systems. In addition, its multi-vessel simulation capabilities have potential applications in coastal surveillance, search-and-rescue operations and maritime defence. AI Agents.content: # Zendesk Readies For An Agent-To-Agent Service World Zendesk’s newly launched AI Outcome Platform and the company’s expanded use of an outcome pricing model all anticipate customer service increasingly becoming an agentic AI operation. Zendesk is preparing for the not-too-distant future when agentic customer service applications respond to personal agents as often as they support real people. This week, Zendesk launched the AI Outcome Platform, a new offering that connects internal customer support tools with external AI assistants. The company also announced its expanded use of an unlimited-seats, outcome-focused pricing plan that replaces traditional seat-based fees. Shashi Upadhyay (pictured), Zendesk president of product, engineering and AI, predicted in an interview with CRN that in just a couple of years more than 50 percent of the traffic around customer service within businesses and organizations will be agent-to-agent. [Related: Driving AI Transformation: The 2026 CRN AI 100] “We’re seeing a pretty big shift in the world of customer experience and, specifically, in customer service,” Upadhyay said. “The big shift is that AI agents have been taking over, have become more and more capable, so they’re able to actually take over a lot of routine—and sometimes even more complex—tasks. The interactions shift from people-to-people to AI-to-AI.” He noted that a significant driver is the growing use of personal agents such as Instinct and Meta Muse to handle personal tasks. “Our view is that everyone in the world is going to have a personal agent who’s going to do real work for them,” Upadhyay said. “Real work means everything from, you know, booking flight tickets, to getting hotel reservations, to shopping for them—solving problems for them.” That will include contacting call centers and service desks to resolve billing errors, return merchandise, update personal information, and so on. And that will include seeking assistance from systems like Zendesk. “So, it’ll be from personal agents being asked to do a job, and then a company’s agents, the service agents, actually doing the job,” he said. The Outcome AI Platform, what Upadhyay described as an evolution of Zendesk’s flagship platform, “brings people, AI agents, apps, teams, everything together to better understand context—the intent of the human who wants a problem solved—complete work across the system, verify work across the system, and then learn from them,” the executive said. The Outcome AI Platform incorporates a number of new and existing Zendesk technologies. Most prominent is the Open Service Directory (OSD) that enables personal AI assistants to locate brands’ verified support channels, regardless of whether or not the brand uses Zendesk. OSD also includes an open specification and public directory. Also new in the platform is Zendesk Bridge, which connects external AI agents and interfaces, including ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot and custom internal bots, directly to Zendesk’s service platform, including its AI, service context, workflows and actions. That, according to the company, allows customers to resolve issues using Zendesk data without leaving the AI tools they already use. Also new are specialized AI agents for resolving complex customer and employee tasks using deep domain logic, and the Self-Improving Zendesk feature that helps teams continuously identify and resolve root-cause problems. “Zendesk’s Outcome AI Platform is a natural extension of the work we've been doing together,” said Allison Johnson, Amazon Web Services director of Americas Technology Partners, in an email response to CRN questions. Zendesk and AWS maintain a deep development and go-to-market alliance under a Strategic Collaboration Agreement (SCA) announced in December 2025. “Zendesk customers already use Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Connect to automate up to 80 percent of customer service interactions, and the Outcome AI Platform builds on that foundation as AI moves from answ...

AI Agents.content: UPDATED 16:22 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026 ### Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in funding. The startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC. Mirendil was launched last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM, a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pre-training projects. Pre-training is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow. Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company says that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents. Large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically. Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil says that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete. The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality. The LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or ten times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half million lines of code. Fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the company previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil plans to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs. ##### Image: Unsplash # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. GrubMarket, a South San Francisco, California-based software-as-a-service (SAAS) company working with food producers, wholesalers, distributors and retailers, is expanding its use of artificial intelligence (AI) with a new AI agent. The company designed its new AI agent to turn vendor invoices and receipts into purchase orders for food distributors. The tool, called the “AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent,” was made to reduce the amount of manual data entry required from produce and other fresh food distributors. “The food supply chain industry is undergoing unprecedented transformation driven by artificial intelligence,” said Mike Xu, CEO of GrubMarket, in a release statement. “With our new AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent, we are bringing powerful AI capabilities to another critical function within food distribution.” The new agent follows other recent AI rollouts from GrubMarket. In June, the company announced the [launch of an AI sales agent](https://www.digitalcommerce360.com/2026/06/10/grubmarket-ai-agent-for-sales-team/). Its other AI deployments have included a reporting AI agent on its GrubAssist AI platform. GrubMarket also created its Monitoring AI Agent that tracks financial and operational data for customers. Now, the technology provider is turning to purchase orders. ## Why GrubMarket launched its new AI agent Xu said that by automating purchasing workflows, GrubMarket is helping distributors operate more efficiently. In turn, he believes that they can gain better visibility into their businesses, making better-informed decisions and improving profitability. “This launch represents another important step in our broader vision of building specialized AI agents that automate and optimize every major function across the food supply chain industry,” Xu said, adding that the company remains committed to leveraging artificial intelligence to help businesses modernize their operations and unlock new levels of efficiency and growth. LLMs.content: [Ai2](/) # XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question November 13, 2026 Ai2 --- [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06842)[Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/XYBench-dataset)[Code](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench) Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing [**XYBench**](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench), a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the *XY problem*: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: *recognizing* when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately *redirecting* them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. ### Building XYBench We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context. For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem. ### Evaluating how an answer helps A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem. A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. The company said evaluations should assess whether responses raise or lower the likelihood of harm rather than what a model can do, and argued that refusal rates alone are a poor gauge, since declining to engage with a user in crisis is itself a failure. It also called for multidisciplinary evaluation teams, sandboxed testing without internet access, multi-turn conversation tests, human validation of AI graders and published statistical uncertainty, and said it had hardened its own testing environments after incidents. ##### Key Elements ![Anthropic Says AI Safety Scores Can Mislead, Urges Overhaul of Model Testing](https://img.biggo.com/qpR9IwMwEP4cX84OeLk2aMJ6Gr76UV8CcTwgLbojouY/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExLzE4NjA3YTA5LTViMDgtNGMyNy1hOWZhLTczYzFhMGMzMzkyNF8xNzk0NjAzNTE3X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Anthropic is pushing back on the way the AI industry certifies model safety, arguing in a research post published Friday that a favorable score on a safety test tells you little unless the test itself was built to measure the right thing. The company, a leading developer of large language models, said decisions about whether a system is ready to ship, what guardrails it needs and where future safety work should focus all rest on the quality of the evaluations behind them. Its recommendations cover evaluation design, testing environments, grading and the reporting of results. The core problem, as Anthropic frames it, is that a safety claim carries no more weight than the evaluation supporting it. "When we say a model is 'safer than its predecessor,' we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built," the company wrote. "But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build." **Tests that measure capability instead of harm** Anthropic argues that safety evaluations should be judged on whether a model's responses make harm more or less likely, not simply on what the model can do. It points to the concept of construct validity: a test has to actually capture the behavior developers want to prevent. Refusal rates are a case in point. A model that declines every question about suicide and self-harm could look exemplary on a refusal-based metric while leaving a person in crisis without support or a nudge toward human help. "When a user is in crisis, simply declining to engage is, itself, a failure," the company wrote. The same logic applies in biology and cybersecurity. Anthropic said an appropriate response in those domains is rarely a flat refusal; models should engage with legitimate requests while withholding operational details that could enable misuse. Evaluations, in its view, need to capture both a model's willingness to comply with harmful requests and its tendency to reject harmless ones. The company also flagged weaknesses that make existing tests easy to game and hard to reproduce. Results can shift on seemingly minor design choices, such as whether a question is multiple-choice or open-ended, or how the answer options are ordered. **Testing can create its own risk** Anthropic acknowledged that safety testing is not risk-free. Some evaluations run with standard safeguards switched off so that a model's baseline behavior can be observed, which can let a system reach beyond its intended testing environment. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Comprehensive Scoping Survey Maps Capabilities and Gaps in Autonomous AI Coding Agents ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Comprehensive Scoping Survey Maps Capabilities and Gaps in Autonomous AI Coding Agents](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/stackrss-featured-9753-750x422-bio-b0b40891cdcb-750w.webp) Comprehensive Scoping Survey Maps Capabilities and Gaps in Autonomous AI Coding Agents A comprehensive structured scoping survey published in Data Science and Engineering synthesizes five years of research into artificial intelligence coding agents, charting their shift from simple token completion tools toward systems capable of multi-step repository navigation, tool execution, and iterative defect repair. Conducted by researchers including Yanshu Wang, Chenfeng Yang, Shuyang Hou, Xinye Xu, Bin Cui, Yanbing Jiang, and Tong Yang, the study systematically examines academic literature, tool scaffolds, and commercial ecosystem developments available through February 28, 2026. Rather than claiming exhaustive systematic coverage, the authors characterize their work as a scoping survey grounded in reproducible discovery queries across arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and DBLP, which yielded 18,261 unique deduplicated records before manual qualitative filtering established an analyzed corpus of exactly 154 cited sources. Their central technical conclusion emphasizes that while autonomous coding agents demonstrate verified competencies on curated benchmarks, current architectures exhibit strict boundary constraints, unresolved tool-use failure modes, and highly variable productivity outcomes across practical developer environments. To establish conceptual clarity across an increasingly fragmented field, the survey introduces an analytical five-dimensional taxonomy designed to classify systems without conflating internal computation with supervision policies. The authors organize AI coding systems across interaction paradigm, computational architecture, deployment form, orchestration mode, and human-oversight mode, ensuring that each representative system receives a single primary value per dimension. By treating human oversight as an independent axis rather than an inherent property of computational architecture, the taxonomy resolves earlier classification ambiguities, allowing single-agent systems with strict human approval gates to be distinguished from unconstrained pipelines. The interaction dimension demarcates four operational levels spanning basic token completion, multi-turn conversational coding, bounded multi-step agentic workflows, and speculative lifecycle-wide autonomous targets. The authors emphasize that higher levels of interaction do not indicate empirical maturity, noting that no public evidence establishes reliable end-to-end autonomous software development on production systems. The historical progression documented by the authors traces automated programming from formal program synthesis in the 1960s through statistical code models and search-based automated program repair. The subsequent rise of statistical n-gram models and recurrent neural networks established that source code exhibits natural linguistic regularities, yet these techniques remained confined to short local token sequences. Similarly, first-generation program repair systems such as GenProg revealed that candidate patches frequently satisfied test suites superficially by deleting functionality rather than addressing underlying logical flaws. The survey explains that transformer architectures and large-scale pre-training across vast repositories have fundamentally expanded this design space, allowing models to parse incomplete natural-language requirements, reason across disparate files, and interpret interactive execution feedback. Co-founder Zhang Yiming acknowledged the technology gap with leading American AI companies at an internal meeting while signaling his intent to pursue them over the long haul. According to Bloomberg on the 12th (local time), ByteDance shared plans for the new agent and mid- to long-term development goals at a recent all-hands meeting of its AI organization. At the private gathering attended by researchers and engineers, Zhang said the company has the capability to compete head-on with OpenAI and Anthropic, but that catching up to frontier technology would take until 2029-2030 at the earliest. A ByteDance spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. The new agent is said to resemble Muse, which Meta unveiled in September. Muse combines voice conversation with animated avatars to handle tasks on users' behalf. It keeps running on cloud virtual machines even after users close the app, sending emails, searching for shopping options and making payments, and asks for user confirmation only at critical steps such as transfers or sends. Meta attracted more than 10 million users in North America within six weeks of launch and is expanding Muse's reach to smart glasses and a dedicated device, the Muse Charm. Behind ByteDance's move to offer a Muse-like service is a strategy to secure early users by linking the agent to its own platforms. With massive traffic from TikTok and Douyin, the plan is to attach the agent to existing services and quickly establish it in the market. ByteDance is said to have run an internal project called Spell since April to integrate personal AI agent capabilities into its mobile assistant Doubao. It has not been confirmed, however, whether the upcoming agent is directly tied to the Spell project. The heaviest emphasis in Zhang's remarks was on data. He lamented that the datasets used by Seed, the company's AI research organization, for large language model (LLM) pretraining are "several orders of magnitude" smaller than those of frontier competitors. The judgment is that with the scaling law still governing model performance, a data gap translates directly into a ceiling on intelligence. He also reaffirmed the principle behind the company's technology路线 — its technology roadmap. ByteDance will focus on in-house R&D rather than relying on distillation, in which smaller models are trained on the outputs of larger ones. AI Product.content: UPDATED 18:00 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026 ### Exclusive: Onyx Security brings AI agent governance to Glean’s enterprise AI platform by Duncan Riley AI agent security startup Onyx Security Inc. today announced an integration with enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Glean Technologies Inc. to help enterprises govern the AI agents they build and run on Glean. Onyx and Glean are pitching the integration at companies that are moving quickly to roll out autonomous, connected agents across their departments. Onyx claims, however, that most of them are not yet prepared to manage the risks that agents bring. According to Onyx, security teams now need to keep continuous track of agent access, actions and policy compliance. Under the partnership, Glean provides the platform to build, deploy and operate the agents, while the Onyx secure AI control plane is used to extend governance and security across the AI environment. At the core of the integration is discovery, with Onyx able to inventory every Glean agent and the access and capabilities it holds. Ownership, business purpose and a risk classification can then be assigned to each agent, according to the companies. Enterprise AI governance and compliance policies can also be applied through the integration, after which Onyx continuously assesses changes to the permissions, tools and data access granted to each agent. Intent-aware runtime controls, which Onyx applies to prompts, responses and agent actions, provide protection while the agents are running. Unsafe requests can be blocked outright under the controls. In other cases, the controls are said to steer unintended agent actions back in line with company policy. Centralized audit evidence is also maintained across AI environments. From deployment through ongoing operation and expansion, the companies say, agents fall under a single governance model. “As agents gain greater access and autonomy, security teams need visibility and control over what they can do,” said Gil Elbaz, co-founder and chief AI officer at Onyx, who previously worked under Nvidia Corp.’s chief technology officer. “By combining Glean’s enterprise context with Onyx’s security control plane, customers can govern agent activity consistently and confidently across their AI environment.” Glean regards context and governance as “foundational to making enterprise AI both useful and trustworthy,” according to Zubin Irani, the company’s vice president of partnerships. The Onyx integration is said to build on that foundation as organizations deploy agents across their business. Coming into the partnership, Onyx has raised $153 million to date, including a $113 million Series B round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in July. The company launched in March with $40 million in seed and Series A funding. Glean, for its part, last raised $150 million in a Series F round at a valuation of $7.2 billion in June 2025. AI Product.content: [Algeria](/locations/e6mQwkoq6aM3r9Ax)[Egypt](/locations/brKPNG878bq4mwD2)[Ghana](/locations/8ALPwQ5MlXMNgkjW)[Kenya](/locations/RYKzQenvjdMZd2rO)[Morocco](/locations/1gxnklOvzw74Ymz5)[Nigeria](/locations/QVJBwEr7nDq6Db2G) [South Africa](https://www.itweb.co.za/) BUSINESS TECHNOLOGY MEDIA FOR AFRICA * [Home](/) * / * [South Africa](/locations/K5rW1xL75JMRk6m3) * / * [Business](/categories/dgp45qaGdOg7X9l8) * / * SA AI adoption outpaces business value # SA AI adoption outpaces business value --- ![Staff Writer](https://www.itweb.co.za/static/contributors/persons/2013/03/resized/staff-writer.small.gif) [By Staff Writer, ITWeb Johannesburg, 13 Nov 2026](/contributors/YXGxwQDq1w7lPVoZ) [![Google News preferred source](/google_preferred_source_badge.webp)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=itweb.africa)[![Google News](/google_news_badge.webp)](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqJggKIiBDQklTRWdnTWFnNEtER2wwZDJWaUxtRm1jbWxqWVNnQVAB?hl=en-ZA&gl=ZA&ceid=ZA%3Aen) --- Arthur Goldstuck, MD of World Wide Worx, author and tech analyst. --- Nine in ten large South African organisations now use artificial intelligence (AI), yet far fewer are convinced it delivers business value, according to The SA AI Index 2026. The third edition of the annual study on AI uptake in SA was conducted by World Wide Worx in partnership with Altron [digital](https://pubads.g.doubleclick.net/gampad/clk?id=6759218543&iu=/22684935574/Africa) Business. The study is based on a telephonic survey of 100 decision-makers at South African organisations with more than 200 employees, conducted in October 2026. The findings build on the inaugural 2024 and 2025 editions of the study, which tracked early corporate enthusiasm for generative AI tools alongside mounting concerns over governance, skills shortages and return on investment across SA’s enterprise sector. It shows that the share of large organisations using AI in some form has doubled in two years, from 45% in 2024 to 67% in 2025 and 93% in 2026. Over the same period, the share of users rating its impact on productivity as positive has fallen dramatically: from 96% to 83% in 2025, and now to 51%. Positive ratings for competitiveness fell from 86% in 2025 to 37% this year, and for customer service from 66% to 38%. The study introduces the SA AI Index, a single score from zero to 100 that measures how far an organisation has integrated AI into its business. The Index is built from five pillars. Organisations score highest on deployment (43.8) and adoption (41.8), followed by workforce (37.2) and governance (32.0). Value scores lowest, at 16.6, and it is held down by measurement as much as by results: 73% of organisations have no tools to assess whether AI delivers value, and 71% cannot put a figure on cost savings from AI. Principals of the study say this means going beyond AI tools: running AI in core processes, under formal control, with its value measured and the workforce adapted to it. The average large South African organisation scores 34.3, meaning it has covered about a third of that distance. “AI has gone from novelty to normal in South African business in just two years,” says Arthur Goldstuck, CEO of World Wide Worx. “But using AI and getting value from it are very different things. The early adopters were enthusiasts who went looking for gains. Today almost everyone uses AI, often in a shallow way, and many organisations are discovering that a language model on every desk does not automatically translate into business results.” According to the backers of the study, where AI runs deeper, the picture changes. Among the 30% of organisations with AI operating in a live business process, 80% report a positive effect on productivity, against 44% of those still experimenting and 6% of those using AI only on an ad hoc basis. Chmielewski and Thomas Buckley Bloomberg A century after Walt Disney Co. transfixed moviegoers with a hand-drawn mouse appearing on a silver screen with synchronized sound, the world’s biggest entertainment company is now exploring a new frontier in animation: artificial intelligence. In December, the company will bring Ozzy Fox, a children’s series rendered by AI, to its flagship Disney+ streaming platform. Ozzy Fox, about an orange character who regularly bursts into song, is the product of a year-long collaboration with French startup Animaj, whose AI tools convert artists’ hand-drawn images and text instructions into three-dimensional animation. It’s just one example of a wider mission, led by Chief Executive Officer Josh D’Amaro, to bring the 103-year-old home of Disney princesses, Pixar and Star Wars into the AI era. Just one week into D’Amaro’s tenure as CEO, OpenAI shuttered its Sora text-to-video platform, scuttling a planned three-year partnership that would have seen Disney invest $1 billion into the startup and license more than 200 of its characters for use in AI-generated short videos. Since then, the company has charted its own course and is leaning on artificial intelligence to upgrade every one of its units from finance to film. At the same time, Disney has been looking to cut costs, moves that have resulted in regular rounds of layoffs as the company’s traditional TV channels struggle to retain viewers and advertisers. D’Amaro’s embrace of AI marks a new approach for Disney. Under former CEO Bob Iger, Disney employed the carrot and the stick. It litigated against startups including Midjourney Inc. and MiniMax over alleged copyright infringement, after images featuring Mickey Mouse brandishing a machine gun or crude depictions of Disney princesses appeared on social media, while collaborating with one, OpenAI, which promised to act responsibly. The false start of Disney’s collapsed deal with OpenAI and the threat of AI replacing artists speaks to Hollywood’s struggle to reconcile the promise of cheaper, faster filmmaking with fears that it could undermine the creative talent and intellectual property on which the industry depends. Those concerns fueled the crippling actors’ and writers’ strikes in 2023 and are simmering throughout an economic downturn in Los Angeles. Few companies have more on the line than Disney. After more than $100 billion worth of acquisitions in the past two decades, from Marvel to Pixar, Star Wars owner Lucasfilm and The Simpsons owner 21st Century Fox, Disney has one of the industry’s richest troves of characters, stories and franchises. Disney hasn’t articulated an overall AI strategy,  but teams across the company are experimenting with different applications, hinting at the potential for broad use of the technology.  In September, the company named  Karandeep Anand - a technology veteran who most recently lead an AI startup - as Disney’s first chief technology officer, in a broad signal of the role AI is likely to play in the entertainment giant’s future. Like other Hollywood studios, Disney began by introducing AI in parts of the business where it is least likely to encounter creative resistance. AI Product.content: # Why Silicon Valley’s Knives Came Out for Anthropic Dario Amodei, the company’s chief executive, publicly frets about the dangers of artificial intelligence and has made enemies of his peers along the way. Credit...Timo Lenzen Supported by By Kalley HuangMike Isaac and Cecilia Kang Kalley Huang and Mike Isaac reported from San Francisco, and Cecilia Kang from Washington. Jensen Huang and Satya Nadella had a problem. Anthropic and OpenAI, the leading artificial intelligence companies, were lobbying the White House to prevent some A.I. models from being developed and widely shared because, they argued, they were too dangerous. But Mr. Huang and Mr. Nadella’s companies, Nvidia and Microsoft, saw those A.I. models as a big business opportunity. At the end of July, Mr. Huang — who resigned from his job on Thursday after Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into his conduct — and Mr. Nadella intervened. They emailed each other drafts of a letter saying those A.I. models should remain open, according to four people familiar with the discussions. When they asked other technology executives whether they’d like to sign on, two dozen companies quickly agreed before the letter became public. Over the next week, 200 more companies — including a chastened OpenAI — signed onto the letter. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, refused. Dr. Amodei has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A.I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever later this month. Along the way, Anthropic — which has cultivated an image as a company that tries to do the right thing — has also gained a reputation for playing hardball with customers and competitors. It has cut some off from its service and lobbied against other companies’s free alternatives to its A.I. Over the last year, other technology companies and investors have organized to push back, according to more than 20 people in the technology industry, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve their relationships with Anthropic. They have tried to show a united front to counter Dr. Amodei’s warnings about A.I. They have leaned on their ties to President Trump to keep regulators away. They have publicly complained about Anthropic’s business practices. They have even spoken with another Anthropic executive about Dr. Amodei scaring people with his rhetoric. ## Related Content Advertisement

While AI technology can help companies improve efficiency, reduce costs, and streamline operations, working with an AI vendor may raise legal and commercial issues that should be addressed before entering into an agreement. Companies may want to look beyond a vendor’s technology and consider its experience, data practices, legal compliance, and contractual protections before entering into an agreement. **Vendor Experience and Expertise** Before selecting an AI vendor, key areas to evaluate include the vendor’s experience, qualifications, and track record. For example, does the vendor have a team of qualified engineers, AI specialists, and data scientists capable of developing, maintaining, and supporting technology? Another diligence focus is the vendor’s litigation history. Companies may want to research whether the vendor has been involved in intellectual property infringement claims, data privacy disputes, or other litigation involving its technology. This information can help identify potential risks and inform negotiations over contractual protections, including indemnification obligations and limitations of liability. **Data Privacy and Security** When selecting a vendor and a particular AI solution, it is important to consider the ways in which an AI vendor collects, uses, stores, and protects data, particularly when the AI technology will process confidential company information, personal information, or other sensitive data. Additional questions to consider include whether the vendor has the necessary rights to use its AI training data, including any publicly available or scraped datasets, and whether it intends to use customer inputs or AI-generated outputs to train or improve its models. Understanding the source of training data and the vendor’s rights to use it can help assess potential legal risks. When negotiating an AI vendor agreement, companies may want to consider the following types of provisions, taking into account the applicable data in scope and the functionality of the applicable solution: * Limiting the vendor’s use of customer data to the purposes authorized under the agreement. * Restricting the vendor from using confidential or proprietary information to train its AI models without the customer’s consent. * Requiring appropriate data security measures and notification of security incidents. * Addressing the return or deletion of customer data upon termination of the agreement. **Quality of Output, Transparency, and Bias** Generative AI models have the potential to produce inaccurate, incomplete, or biased results, which may create legal, financial, or reputational risks depending on how the technology is used. They share a label and almost nothing else. Mistral publishes a named license (the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral describes as a modified MIT license), while a [third-party comparison of open-weight licenses](https://gpuwerk.com/blog/open-weight-model-licenses/) flags that several rivals need a closer read of the model card before you ship anything on top of them. That gap matters more than a benchmark point. A team that picks the wrong route to a model, whether a vendor API, a hyperscaler catalog or its own GPUs, can end up with a bill, a latency profile or a legal question it did not plan for. Our [self-hosted versus API cost breakdown](https://shattered.io/self-hosted-llm-vs-api-kimi-k3-1-pro-glm-5-3-deepseek-v4-1-mistral-large-4-2026/) covers the hardware arithmetic. The question here is different: for each of the five current open source AI models, which routes exist today, what does each route cost, and what does the official evidence actually confirm? Everything below is dated November 13, 2026. Where an official page confirms a fact, the text says so. Where only a third-party tracker or a forum post supports it, the text says that too, and the table cells stay empty rather than guess. That discipline is the point. The open-model market moves weekly, and a confident but wrong spec costs readers real money. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Open Source AI Models Actually Mean in 2026 Strictly speaking, almost none of these releases are open source in the way the software industry uses the term. The usual bar covers code, data and the freedom to modify and redistribute. What the labs ship is closer to open weights: a downloadable set of parameters, usually with a license that grants some rights and withholds others. Moonshot AI officially calls Kimi K3.1 Pro open-weight, and Mistral calls Large 4 open weight. Neither claims a fully open training pipeline. This comparison uses the phrase open source ai models the way readers do while keeping the distinction visible. When a sentence says open source, read it as weights you can download under some license. When it says open-weight, the lab itself used that word. ### The evidence ladder Not every claim deserves equal trust. We sort the evidence into four rungs and place each model on the ladder: * **Rung 1, official page confirms:** the lab’s own announcement, documentation or pricing page states the fact. * **Rung 2, official page implies:** the lab uses the phrase open-weight or open models without naming a license file. * **Rung 3, third-party tracker:** a pricing or license aggregator reports it, and no official page contradicts it. * **Rung 4, forum or single mention:** a user post or one-off report. Treat it as a lead, not a fact. Mistral Large 4 sits mostly on rung 1. Mistral’s announcement of the open-weight release names the license and its version (v26.10). Both models are open to Copilot Pro+, Max, Business and Enterprise users in VS Code, Visual Studio and Copilot CLI, and both can be picked for the Copilot coding agent. The price of entry is clear. GitHub lists Pro+ at $39 a month and Max at $100 a month, and agent work now draws down a pool of AI credits where one credit equals one cent. GitHub’s own materials now treat that description as outdated. On October 28, 2026, the company announced a connected Copilot cloud experience, and the rollout began the same day. Under it, a developer can start a cloud agent session from a phone, steer it from VS Code, and check the result on GitHub.com. That is a different product shape. The open-source GitHub Next project lets a team describe automation in plain Markdown, which compiles into GitHub Actions YAML. Tasks such as issue triage, CI-failure analysis, documentation updates and test writing run inside Actions, using Copilot or another coding agent. It is the clearest sign that GitHub wants agents running on its infrastructure, not just in a developer’s editor. So the model additions of the past week land on a platform that was already reorganizing around agents. TrnRT is an open inference engine for running large language models on Trainium hardware. It combines model execution, caching and an API server in a system designed for teams that compile models on a host and serve them on Trainium. ![The README of the RunanywhereAI/trnrt repository on GitHub](https://news.lavx.hu/api/media/file/runanywhereai-trnrt-readme-2026-11-13.jpg) *Screenshot: the project's README on GitHub* ## What it is TrnRT runs large language model inference on Trainium hardware and serves responses through an API compatible with chat and text-completion clients. The project focuses on the serving path: it includes an inference engine, a request router, caches and a compile pipeline. Its README identifies GLM-5.3-Flash as its first supported model, with support for more open models planned. The project targets teams that want to run model inference on this hardware and connect it to existing client workflows. The engine is built around a model's decode workload, where it generates output after processing a prompt. TrnRT groups the work into kernels designed for Trainium, then routes requests to engines that maintain session state. Its API supports chat and completion requests, streaming responses, tool calls and reasoning output. That combination lets an application use familiar request patterns while TrnRT handles model execution and the hardware-specific serving path. ## How it works TrnRT uses NKI megakernels for decode. Each kernel fuses work across part of a model layer, including attention, mixture-of-experts processing and other model operations. The README says this design keeps working data in on-chip memory, uses the chip's physical cores in a balanced way and places collective operations inside the kernel. These choices address the instruction overhead and kernel boundaries that the project identifies as limits on decode performance. A compile pipeline prepares model graphs on a CPU host before serving. The serving machine loads those compiled artifacts, so the default serving process does not compile graphs at startup. At runtime, a session-affine router keeps a conversation with the same engine, allowing that engine to reuse cached prompt prefixes. TrnRT stores cache data across device and host memory, including evicted pages and state checkpoints, to support reuse across requests. ## Key features The prefix cache uses a radix tree to organize key-value pages and retains a host-memory tier for data that leaves device memory. Open Source AI.titleZh: llama.cpp 1.0 reaches stable release for local AI
Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) [tbreak.](/) [Tech](https://tbreak.com/tech/)/[AI](https://tbreak.com/topics/ai/)/[PC](https://tbreak.com/topics/pc/) # llama.cpp reaches version 1.0 for local AI tools The engine behind many local AI setups will flag breaking changes with major-version numbers, so app makers can plan for them. [Tbreak Editor](https://tbreak.com/author/tbreak/) Change language to 0:00 The open-source engine many local AI setups run on, llama.cpp, reached 1.0 on 13 November. Its maintainers now promise app developers that breaking changes will come only with major-version bumps. According to the [ggml-org post on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/llama-cpp-v1), the project has grown a lot in the 3.5 years since it started. The post notes that “many downstream applications already depend on our work.” For an app maker, a breaking change now shows up in the version number, so they can plan for it. > Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount. > > The ggml-org team, Hugging Face blog post ## Subscribe to our Newsletters for more Tech Stories Found us on Google? [Add tbreak as a preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tbreak.com) to see more of our stories in Top Stories. ## What llama.cpp 1.0 actually promises llama.cpp runs AI models; it isn’t a model itself. Two libraries reached v1.0.0 on 13 November 2026: llama.cpp (*libllama*, which handles LLM inference in C/C++) and ggml (*libggml*, the tensor library underneath it). Both now follow semantic versioning, with three kinds of release: * **Major:** a breaking change to the public C API. * **Minor:** a backward-compatible feature, backend update, new model support, or API addition. * **Patch:** a bug fix with no API change. The post says both projects “will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps.” The API is the interface developers use to call the libraries, while the ABI is the binary interface compiled apps rely on. Superpower Daily sums it up as “a signal for downstream teams, not a freeze on change.” ## What changed in the release The 1.0 release also cleared out old code. [Unite.AI’s reading](https://www.unite.ai/llama-cpp-v1-0-0-sets-api-stability-rules-for-local-ai-tools/) of the [GitHub release notes](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/v1.0.0) says it removes the deprecated public API, including 35 deprecated functions. It also moves the NextN speculative-decoding API from llama-ext.h into the public llama.h header. Unite.AI also lists new functionality: * **Memory:** FP8 key-value caches, plus a host-memory cache for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with a configurable CPU share. * **Models:** Kimi-K3.1-Pro, Ripple, xing4\_0 text, drama-3 text-to-speech, and vision for MageVL-Cowork and Kimi-K3.1. * **Server:** fixes for server-side request forgery, CORS, and DNS rebinding; HF\_TOKEN restricted to huggingface.co hosts; and a new OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech endpoint. * **Web interface:** named chat groups and a live-preview Markdown editor. * **Mobile:** layouts that use device safe areas and full-screen dialogues, as well as an Android chat editor that can open the virtual keyboard. Unite.AI says an official llama.cpp release tag is created only when its internal copy of ggml matches the released ggml, so system-wide installs through Debian and Homebrew stay compatible. ## Where it runs The maintainers say ggml “is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence.” It uses dedicated backends that can load at runtime. llama.cpp currently supports more than 150 architecture variants, as well as all mainstream speculative-decoding methods. Pre-release builds cover Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, and iOS, with other channels including Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, MacPorts, Winget, and an XCFramework for iOS and macOS. PHOTO: REUTERS ![avatar-alt](https://cassette.sphdigital.com.sg/image/straitstimes/ef286047322a1d87a248de232b0f3326eaafbee83afbb2d412f29d35c0e6cb86?w=150) Sarah Koh Published Nov 13, 2026, 02:46 PM Updated Nov 13, 2026, 03:23 PM SINGAPORE - Once known for [primarily](/world/united-states/why-nvidia-matters-and-whats-now-at-stake?ref=inline-article) [supplying](/world/united-states/why-nvidia-matters-and-whats-now-at-stake?ref=inline-article) [the video game industry,](/world/united-states/why-nvidia-matters-and-whats-now-at-stake?ref=inline-article) US chipmaker Nvidia’s pivot to meet the unrelenting demands of artificial intelligence has made it indispensable to the global economy. However, its dominance is now being tested following the resignation of its chief executive Jensen Huang, [triggered by revelations of extramarital affairs,](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/former-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-had-a-relationship-with-a-second-employee-sources-say?ref=inline-article) including with a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The company continues to dominate the artificial intelligence (AI) computing market and remains one of the biggest beneficiaries of rising AI infrastructure spending. NVIDIA’s powerful graphics processing units (GPUs), networking products and full-stack AI platforms have become essential for companies building and operating AI data centers. With hyperscale cloud providers, AI startups, enterprises and governments increasing their investments in AI infrastructure, NVIDIA appears well-positioned to deliver another strong quarter. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Data Center revenues jumped 117% year over year and 18% sequentially to a record $89.02 billion. The growth was driven by strong demand for its Blackwell Ultra infrastructure, with both hyperscale and AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise (ACIE) customers contributing significantly. This positive trend is expected to have continued in the third quarter. One of the biggest growth drivers could be continued investments by hyperscale cloud providers. During the last earnings call, NVIDIA's management noted that the cloud industry's backlog exceeded $2 trillion, while capital expenditures by the top five hyperscalers are expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027. Amazon Web Services has also announced plans to deploy an additional 2 million NVIDIA GPUs between the third quarter of fiscal 2027 and the second quarter of fiscal 2029. These investments should have supported demand for NVIDIA's computing platforms in the third quarter. Another important growth driver is the rising demand from AI startups, enterprises, sovereign customers and regional cloud providers. In the second quarter, ACIE revenues surged 138% year over year and 25% sequentially to $40.31 billion. Growth was driven by additional capacity from NeoCloud providers, rising enterprise and AI startup demand, and hyperscalers purchasing AI cloud capacity to supplement their own infrastructure. This diversified customer base is anticipated to have supported Data Center growth in the third quarter. The ramp-up of NVIDIA's latest products is likely to have provided another boost. The company has commenced production shipments of its next-generation Vera Rubin platform and expects it to account for approximately 20% of Data Center revenues in the third quarter.
